Why Reddit (RDDT) Shares Are Falling Today
What Happened?

Shares of online community and discussion platform Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) fell 3.4% in the afternoon session after the European Union officially added the company to its strictest regulatory tier under the Digital Services Act because its user base exceeded 45 million monthly active users in the bloc.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Reddit has been designated as a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP), a classification that requires the company to comply with stricter anti-harm standards and systemic risk assessments by the end of December 2026 or face penalties of up to 6% of its annual global revenue. The enhanced oversight gives the European Commission investigative powers to probe the inner workings of the platform's algorithms and content moderation practices.

After the initial drop, the shares shed some of the losses and rose to $148.08, down 3.2% from the previous close.

The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks. Is now the time to buy Reddit? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.

What Is The Market Telling Us

Reddit's shares are extremely volatile and have had 54 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 6 days ago when the stock gained 4.9% after The Information reported that Meta Platforms is preparing to launch a consumer AI agent named Hatch that is trained to access and browse the social discussion platform. 

According to coverage of the upcoming launch, Hatch will allow users to navigate Reddit, order from DoorDash, shop on Etsy, check Yelp, and manage Microsoft Outlook directly inside Meta's ecosystem.

Meta plans to launch the tool in the coming weeks and has weighed tiered pricing that could include a premium subscription of up to $199.99 per month. 

The inclusion of Reddit alongside core utility apps highlights the platform's unique position in the broader AI landscape. As tech giants shift from basic chatbots to action-oriented agents, access to Reddit's vast repository of human opinions, recommendations, and real-time community knowledge is increasingly viewed as a foundational layer for these new ecosystems.

Reddit is down 38.8% since the beginning of the year, and at $148.08 per share, it is trading 45.3% below its 52-week high of $270.71 from September 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Reddit's shares at the IPO in March 2024 would now be looking at an investment worth $2,936.

title: Reddit Has Been One of the Worst Stocks in the S&P 500. Here's Why It's a Buy.
detail:
Reddit Has Been One of the Worst Stocks in the S&P 500. Here's Why It's a Buy.
Marc Guberti, The Motley Fool

Reddit (NYSE: RDDT) has had a bad year. Its stock is down by more than 30% year-to-date, making it one of the worst-performing stocks in the S&P 500.

However, that doesn't mean Reddit is doing poorly as a company. In fact, now looks like a good buying opportunity. Reddit's year-to-date performance does not align with its fundamentals.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Reddit's financials are soaring

A lagging stock price does not always indicate poor fundamentals, and Reddit is a good example. The social media company's revenue soared by 61% year over year in its second quarter. Net income also almost tripled year over year.

These aren't one-off results, either. This was Reddit's eighth consecutive quarter of delivering more than 60% year-over-year revenue growth. Reddit is making some money by letting artificial intelligence training companies use its data, but almost all of its revenue still comes from online ads.

Its advertising segment was up 64% year over year, and accounted for roughly 95% of Reddit's total revenue. Growth and rising margins enabled Reddit to repurchase $235 million in shares in the quarter.

This growth is built on more users joining the platform

An 18% year-over-year boost in daily active users demonstrates that the current momentum is sustainable. Some companies scramble to raise advertising costs and set fees to achieve higher revenue growth as user growth declines. However, a user base built on healthy growth makes it easier for Reddit to realize high growth rates without penny-pinching its advertisers.

It's not just daily active users that are on the upswing, either. Reddit closed the quarter with 514.6 million weekly active users, which was a 24% year-over-year increase.

Reddit trades at a 30.5 forward P/E ratio, which isn't too far off from Meta Platforms' (NASDAQ: META) 19 forward P/E ratio when considering their fundamental progress. Meta Platforms delivered only 28% year-over-year revenue growth and a 3% year-over-year uptick in daily active users.

Reddit already trades at a premium to Meta Platforms, but it's fair to argue that Reddit may deserve a higher premium. Its net income is also growing at a much faster rate than Facebook's parent company, implying that its forward P/E ratio will quickly become more attractive than its current level.

For most people, investment income doesn't have to replace a paycheck to be useful. A few hundred dollars a month could take care of utilities, while $1,000 or more could cover a mortgage, groceries or several other major expenses.

That was the idea behind a recent discussion on Reddit's r/dividends community, where one person asked whether investors were using dividends as a meaningful second income alongside their jobs. The responses ranged from people collecting less than $100 a month to others saying their portfolios now generate thousands.

From Paying the Electric Bill to Replacing a Part-Time Job

One 58-year-old said they receive about $500 a month from less than $100,000 invested in dividend stocks and hope to reach at least $1,000 a month. They plan to retire next year with about $6,000 a month in pretax retirement income, eventually supplemented by Social Security.

Another commenter said $1,000 a month was also their target, while others were already using dividends to supplement retirement income. One retiree said they were using dividends from a Roth IRA alongside Social Security, showing how investment income can fill the gap without replacing a full paycheck.

Others are already bringing in considerably more. One commenter said they earn $2,000 a month in dividend income while also working part-time as a self-employed worker. Another said they moved money from a high-yield savings account into dividend-paying investments and watched their monthly income climb from between $200 and $300 to $1,800. They said that, at their current pace, the dividends could cover all their bills within nine months.

Another investor of the same age said they were approaching $2,000 a month and hoped to eventually reach $4,000, at which point they could work part-time.

Reddit stock has had a weak start to the year, with the share price down 36.7% year to date, while broad valuation checks suggest the stock is not a clear bargain at current levels.

The year to date decline of 36.7% raises the question of whether Reddit is now priced for too much caution or simply moving closer to a fairer trading range.

The recent focus on Reddit content within Meta's planned Hatch AI agent can support long term monetisation hopes, while the key risk is that content licensing and data economics do not translate into sustained cash flow strength.

With a value score of 2 out of 6, Reddit stock currently screens as leaning expensive rather than a straightforward value opportunity on the broader checks.

The issue now is whether Reddit's current price fairly reflects its data and platform potential or still builds in too much optimism after a difficult year to date.

Where Does Reddit Sit on Earnings?

P/E is a useful yardstick for Reddit because earnings are now positive and investors can compare what they are paying per dollar of profit to other interactive media stocks.

Reddit currently trades on a P/E of 33.8x, which is close to a peer average of 32.1x and well above the broader Interactive Media and Services industry average of 13.5x. On Simply Wall St's fair multiple framework, a P/E of 33.3x would be in line with Reddit's current mix of growth expectations, margins, size and risks, so the live multiple is only slightly above that reference point. The recent interest around Meta's planned Hatch AI agent and Reddit content has lifted attention on the stock, yet the P/E still clusters near the modelled fair range rather than moving away dramatically.

On the P/E multiple, Reddit stock currently appears to be trading at roughly fair value compared with its tailored fair ratio and closer peers.

On the Aug. 25 episode of Mad Money, Jim Cramer responded to a lightning round caller asking about a potential Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) and Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) tie-up with a direct call: "I think Reddit is such a buy at $166. It's ridiculously cheap. So with or without synergy with Netflix, you've got what I regard as a buy."

ojbyrne / Flickr

The stock he was talking about, Reddit, closed at $162.45 on Aug. 25 and has been one of the most punished growth names of 2026. But the gap between Cramer's call and the tape is the whole story. Reddit is down nearly 35% year to date and down more than 25% over the past year, even as the underlying business continues to compound at a pace few public companies can match.

A Business Growing 61%, a Stock Falling 29%

Reddit's Q2 2026 press release, filed July 30, laid out numbers that do not square with a 29% drawdown. Revenue rose 61.1% to $804.9 million, easily topping the $731 million consensus. EPS of $1.25 beat by 29.23%, marking the fifth straight quarter Reddit has cleared Street estimates. Net income more than doubled to $252.8 million, and adjusted EBITDA margin came in at 42.6%.

Advertising revenue jumped 64% to $762 million. Global ARPU climbed 36% to $6.18, and U.S. ARPU rose 51% to $11.85. On the call, CFO Drew Vollero pointed out that "Reddit grew more than 60% for the eighth consecutive quarter while operating cash flow adjusted EBITDA, net income, and GAAP EPS all more than doubled in the quarter year over year."

Reddit's Balance Sheet Agrees With Cramer
RDDT Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.

The company's own capital allocation is the strongest supporting evidence for the "ridiculously cheap" thesis. In Q2, Reddit repurchased 1.5 million Class A shares at an average price of $157.57 under a $235 million program, with roughly $760 million remaining under authorization. Cash and marketable securities stood at $2.8 billion. Management is buying the same stock at nearly the same price Cramer flagged.
